title: Learn a piece from a recording
summary: Learn a short piece by ear from a recording only, with no sheet music for it at all.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil
a recording of a short piece with no sheet music for it

figure.alt: A row of twelve boxes, standing for the twelve bars of the piece learned by ear from a recording, four bars added each sitting with no sheet music to check against.

steps.title: Learn a piece from a recording
steps.body:
Every piece so far started on a page. This one starts as sound only. That is how most musicians actually learn what they play: by ear, from hearing it, with no page to check against.

1. Listen to the recording all the way through, twice, with no keys touched at all.
2. Find the first four bars by ear, checking each note against the recording as many times as it takes.
3. Add four more bars each sitting, always checking against the recording, never guessing and moving on.
4. On the last sitting, play as much as you have learned, then compare it once more to the recording for anything you missed.

Learning without a page forces your ear to do work that reading usually does for you. That work makes every other kind of listening sharper.

figure.alt: The same twelve boxes, the first four shaded for what sitting one finds by ear, the rest added four at a time in the sittings that follow.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: listen twice, find the first four bars by ear
Sitting 2: check those four bars, then add four more
Sitting 3: check everything so far, then add four more bars
Sitting 4: play everything learned, compare once more to the recording
An old piece played once, from the page, for contrast

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Play the recording once, then play as much of the piece as you have learned by ear, hands in the frame.

extras.title: Write down a tune from your head
extras.body:
Pick a tune only you know, hum it once, then work out its notes on the keys by ear.

Start with a question: could someone else play your tune just from the notes you write down?

Three constraints: keep it to four bars, use notes you can name, and mark the rhythm as well as the pitch.

Sketch first: write the note names and rhythm on paper before checking them against your memory of the tune.

You know it works when someone else can play it back correctly from your page alone.
